column11: Why do biliary hamartomas appear as small cystic lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree?
column12: Biliary hamartomas result from embryologic failure of normal bile-duct formation. The malformed ductal structures remain as small benign cystic foci rather than forming patent ducts, explaining their small irregular cyst-like appearance and lack of communication with the biliary tree. This duct-development mechanism is the key imaging pivot separating them from Caroli disease.

column11: What anatomic mechanism produces the central-dot sign in Caroli disease?
column12: Caroli disease is saccular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts. Small portal-vein and hepatic-artery branches remain within/bridge the dilated ducts, so on contrast-enhanced CT they appear as a central enhancing dot surrounded by fluid-filled ductal dilatation. The sign therefore reflects vascular radicles traversing abnormally dilated communicating bile ducts.

column11: Why can focal hepatic fat mimic a cyst on CT yet be distinguished on opposed-phase MRI?
column12: Focal fat can become very low attenuation on CT and may approach water attenuation. Core explains that when fat and water protons occupy the same voxel, their signals subtract on out-of-phase gradient imaging, producing signal loss. Thus opposed-phase signal drop confirms intracellular fat rather than true simple fluid, which is the key cyst-mimic discriminator.

column15: What ultrasound findings are classic for hepatic hydatid disease?

column15: What imaging features define Caroli disease and separate it from noncommunicating hepatic cysts?

Saccular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts.
